title: HexOct: The Hexagonality Law — with the Window Law, the Rule of Halves & the Swap Rule
description:
Version 7, third edition (1 November 2026), subtitled with the Window Law, the Rule of Halves & the Swap Rule, adds Part IV, The Window Law (Chapter 15, from #84, DICTO DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23848832), and reads the whole book within it. Whatever a stacking fixes through a window of g neighbouring layers averages to a linear function of the shares of its c/h words of length g. The book states how the rules fit together, in the opening and again in the epilogue with the proofs cited: the Window Law always holds, for every window g; the Rule of Halves and the Swap Rule decide which window a count needs; when a count needs only one layer, or two layers and obeys the Swap Rule, the Window Law reduces to the Hexagonality Law (g = 1), the straight line in hexagonality; pair counts that break the Swap Rule are planes in h and the share of neighbouring hexagonal pairs. New: the Hexagonality Law defined as a law of structural crystallography, with its reach stated exactly; one sentence in each affected chapter conclusion; new notation, epilogue rows and an open problem; a new cover. 113 pages.

Version 6, second edition (31 October 2026), added thirteen full-page plates after Chapter 14: the two tiles, HexOct-K, seven stackings built from the tiles (3C, 2H, 4H, 6H, 9R, Fibonacci and random), Chucky, Fang and the Triskelion Tetrahedron. 92 pages.

The Law gave the pieces, / The pieces prove the law. (DICTO)

Version 5 is retitled HexOct: The Hexagonality Law (DICTO, 30 October 2026), with the new title on the cover. Versions 2 to 4 were titled HexOct: The Laws of Stacking; the first edition, The Laws of Stacking (28 October 2026), is this record too. Version 4 takes Chapter 14 from #75 version 2, with HexOct-K and the stacking as the clock (keyed tiles that run a cellular automaton, one step per layer), and lists the four books in About the author. Version 3 added the cover, the HexOct square (HEXOCT across and down a 6 × 6 square, each letter on its tile: H, E, X on the h-tile, O, C, T on the c-tile), an About the author page, and sets the whole book in a sans-serif face. A book gathering DICTO's work on close-packed stackings, from the Rule of Halves (#57) to spin ice and kagome magnets (#74) and the two tiles HexOct (#75): fifteen papers as a prologue and fourteen chapters in three parts, with a new opening, an epilogue and an index.

It shows seven things. However equal balls are stacked in close-packed layers, the space is shared out into finitely many kinds of piece, each borrowed whole or in half from the cubic or the hexagonal stacking (the Rule of Halves). When a stacking changes, the pieces change only by swapping: the two mixed pieces add up to the two pure ones (the Swap Rule). For every piece fixed by its two neighbouring layers this is equivalent to the Hexagonality Law: every count and volume is a straight line in the share h of hexagonal layers. The counts that decide real chemistry and physics obey the law exactly in real crystals: hydrogen sites in metals (2 − h), faces shared in perovskites and battery cathodes (2h), eclipsed bonds in diamond, ice and semiconductors (h/2), kagome planes in magnets (1 + 3(1 − h)). Where a property depends on energy, the distance from the straight line is one number per material, sorting them from tin, on the line, to silicon carbide, far from it; in spin ice and water ice the loops that set the frozen-in entropy do not depend on the stacking through every length computed. Every close-packed stacking is a string of two layer tiles only, the c-tile and the h-tile (HexOct), built from the pieces of the Rule of Halves: any tile sits on any tile, flat where the walk weight is at most −7/24 and interlocking above. Part III adds HexOct-K, keyed HexOct tiles: keys on a layer's axis faces make it a Wang tiling, so HexOct-K layers can compute, shown by a four-tile layer that counts in binary. Part IV, the Window Law, holds the laws in one theorem and tests it with exact counts on perovskites, Frank–Kasper phases and the approximants of quasicrystals.

Each chapter is its paper, theorems and proofs word for word, and names the paper and DICTO DOI it comes from; unrelated passages are cut; mentions of papers outside the book link to their DOIs. Sources checked for every chapter are listed in an appendix.

The ideas and names are DICTO's. Computation and proof with Claude (Anthropic). Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. More at dictospheres.com.

Version 8 (6 November 2026) adds Part V, The end of the walk: Chapter 16, Narcissus and Covenant (also paper #98, DICTO DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24005929). In Chapter 4 the opening now reads that DICTO proposed the rules belong not to one structure but to stacking itself.

Version 9 (7 November 2026) adds Part VI, Further results: Chapter 17, The Turned Twin (DICTO's study note of 4 November 2026: every close-packed stacking is a tiling by rhombic dodecahedra and trapezo-rhombic dodecahedra, one per ball, and DICTO's turned node is the twisted ball), and Chapter 18, Locked Layers, the Fibonacci Spectrum and the Rock-Salt Pieces (single HexOct layers interlock; the Fibonacci word's spectrum is pure point while its crystal has no sharp peaks; in rock salt the stacking's freedom lies in the pieces at hexagonal layers, numerical).
